newsitem.title: POLAND: OSCE urges punishment of war rapes in Tribunal.
newsitem.headline: OSCE urges punishment of war rapes in Tribunal.

text.p: The Parliamentary Assembly of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) demanded on Tuesday that rapes committed during the war in former Yugoslavia be thoroughly prosecuted in the International Criminal Tribunal in the Hague.
The assembly of legislators from the OSCE's 54 member countries said charges of rape in the Tribunal had been withdrawn in a number of cases as victims dared not give evidence.

"The Assembly requests the OSCE and participating states to ensure that war crimes in the form of rape are referred to the International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia and are given equal treatment as other grave war crimes," it said in a statement after its four-day session in Warsaw.
The forum also called on its member states to consider torture in the form of rape during armed conflicts as grounds for granting asylum.

The OSCE, rooted in a forum for East-West dialogue set up in the mid-1970s, has in recent years built a role as a monitor of democracy, human rights and arms control, helping with peacekeeping and overseeing elections in fledgling democracies.

It roundly criticised Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko, appealing to him to "restore the rights of the parliament in that country which, having been duly elected on the basis of democratic elections at the end of 1995, is the only rightful parliament there", the statement said.

Lukashenko, who used a landslide win at a referendum last November to shut down parliament and seize vastly wider powers, has cracked down on opponents and the mass media, drawing widespread criticism in the West, especially in Washington.

The OSCE hopes that its Advisory and Monitoring Office, due to start operations in Minsk, will improve the human rights situation in Belarus, the president of the Assembly, Javier Ruperez, told a news conference.

The assembly adopted a declaration calling for intensive work on the so-called Charter on European Security and an OSCE Economic Charter, which would oblige member countries to strengthen security and economic cooperation.

It urged governments to provide access to public information and protect it by law through such mechanisms as a freedom of information act. It backed proposals to appoint an OSCE representative on freedom of the media.
